note: Illustrative candidates written by the lean thread to exercise the three states of lean/eliminate/eliminate.mjs. They are not the open-problems enumerator's candidates (open-problems/candidates.json) and no number here is a measurement; each is a commitment a candidate might make, chosen to show what the formalised theorems can and cannot rule on.

candidates.problem: Could an insect of unchanged proportions be 100 times longer?
candidates.description: A giant insect with the body plan of a 2 cm ant scaled to 2 m, same shape and density, claimed to weigh only 100 times as much.
candidates.source: Galileo's square-cube argument (Two New Sciences, 1638), mass side; lean thread illustration

candidates.problem: Could an insect of unchanged proportions be 100 times longer?
candidates.description: The same giant, correctly weighing 10^6 times as much, claimed to support itself because its legs are also 100 times longer.
candidates.source: Galileo's square-cube argument, strength side (strength scales as L^2); lean thread illustration

candidates.problem: Could an insect of unchanged proportions be 100 times longer?
candidates.description: The same giant, 100 times longer with unchanged proportions and material, claimed able to stand (carry one body weight), given a reference ant whose legs carry 10 body weights (illustrative figure).
candidates.source: Galileo's square-cube argument, strength side, now formalised as R7; lean thread illustration (the safety factor 10 is illustrative, not a measurement)

candidates.problem: Does the neutral molecular clock depend on population size?
candidates.description: A model in which neutral substitutions accumulate at N mu per generation, with N = 1000, so that larger populations evolve faster at neutral sites.

candidates.problem: How often does a new neutral mutation fix?
candidates.description: A claim that a single new neutral mutant among 2000 gene copies fixes about one time in a hundred.

candidates.problem: Can selection for a trait make its mutations fix less often than neutral drift?
candidates.description: A proposed mechanism in which a mutation with a nonnegative selection coefficient, among 10^6 gene copies, fixes with probability at most 10^-9.

candidates.problem: Could a gliding fin become a wing in 10^4 generations?
candidates.description: A design that commits to 10^15 expected substitutions across a 10^9-site genome in 10^4 generations, in a population of 2 x 10^9 gene copies with mutation rate 5 x 10^-9.
candidates.source: lean thread illustration (the quantity 'substitutions a wing requires' is otherwise undefined; this candidate commits to one)

candidates.problem: Can mean fitness fall under constant selection at one locus?
candidates.description: A model of one haploid locus with fixed fitnesses in which mean fitness drops by between 5 and 10 percent of a unit in one generation of selection alone.

candidates.problem: How fast can an asexual mutant spread under the twofold cost?
candidates.description: An asexual lineage at 1 percent of females claimed to reach 50 percent two generations later, with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio.

candidates.problem: How fast can an asexual mutant spread under the twofold cost?
candidates.description: The same lineage claimed to reach 4/103 of females after two generations, which is exactly the fourfold odds the theorem gives.

candidates.problem: Is the generated flying-fish anatomy internally coherent?
candidates.description: The organism thread's emitted blueprint for a flying fish, as a design.
A reading of the claims thread's NHANES result (males, age-bin means 2-19 y, exponent 2.74, CI 2.59 to 2.89) that asserts isometric growth at constant density.
candidates.source: claim-tests/thompson-growth-form/thompson1917-ch03-07/derived/summary.json (exponent and CI); the isometry assertion is the candidate's, not the test's

candidates.problem: Could flying fish become perfectly winged animals?
candidates.description: Darwin's conjecture (Origin, ch. VI) as a candidate with no committed quantities.

candidates.problem: Can a 0.06 kg flying fish glide at 5 m/s?
candidates.description: A claim of steady lift-supported flight at 5 m/s for the physics thread's Cypselurus hiraii specimen L3 (W = 0.5886 N, S = 0.012688 m^2, C_L,max = 0.78, Park and Choi 2010), in air of density 1.225 kg/m^3.
candidates.source: physics/results.json interpretation_B for W, S, C_L,max (Park and Choi 2010 Table 1 model L3); the airspeed 5 m/s and the density 1.225 kg/m^3 are the candidate's commitments, chosen by the lean thread to illustrate C9 (the specimen's v_min is 9.85 m/s)
